2019A16.goal: Thirteen unit circles are packed inside a big circle, all touching where they meet. We need the area inside the big circle but outside the small ones: big area minus $13\pi$. Everything comes down to the big circle's radius.

tools.name: Centres of tangent circles
tools.why: The distance between centres is the sum of the radii.

tools.name: Hexagonal packing
tools.why: Three mutually tangent unit circles have centres forming an equilateral triangle.

tools.name: Height of an equilateral triangle
tools.why: Split it into two $30$-$60$-$90$ triangles.

2019A16.approach: Find the small circle whose centre is farthest from the middle; the big circle touches it, so the big radius is that distance plus $1$. In the hexagonal arrangement the outer six circles sit in the gaps of the first ring, and their centres are at distance $2\sqrt3$ from the centre.

steps.title: Locate the outer centres
steps.explain: The middle circle is surrounded by six circles whose centres are $2$ from the middle, forming a regular hexagon of side $2$. Each outer circle touches two neighbouring circles of that ring, so its centre is the far vertex of an equilateral triangle of side $2$ built on a hexagon side. Its distance from the middle is twice the height of an equilateral triangle of side $2$: $2\cdot\sqrt3=2\sqrt3$.

check.q: What is the height of an equilateral triangle with side $2$?

steps.title: Big radius and area
steps.explain: The big circle touches the outer circles, so its radius is $2\sqrt3+1$ and its area is $\pi(2\sqrt3+1)^2=\pi(13+4\sqrt3)$.

steps.title: Subtract the small circles
steps.explain: The shaded area is $\pi(13+4\sqrt3)-13\pi=4\pi\sqrt3$.

2019A16.bridge: Find the distance to the farthest small centre, add $1$, and subtract $13\pi$ from the big area.
solution: The six inner-ring centres form a hexagon of side $2$ around the middle centre.
Each outer centre is the apex of an equilateral triangle of side $2$ on a hexagon side, at distance $2\sqrt3$ from the middle.
So the big radius is $2\sqrt3+1$ and its area is $\pi(13+4\sqrt3)$.
2019A16.shortcut: Once you see the outer centres at $2\sqrt3$, the $13\pi$ from the small circles cancels the $13\pi$ in the expansion.
traps: Taking the big radius as $3$ or $4$ (stacking circles in a straight line).
Forgetting to add the small radius $1$ to the centre distance.
2019A16.recognize: Packings of equal circles: connect centres to get triangles and hexagons with side $2r$; the bounding circle's radius is the farthest centre distance plus $r$.

2019A17.goal: We build towers of $8$ cubes using at most $2$ red, $3$ blue and $4$ green cubes, so exactly one cube is left out. We count distinct colour sequences of length $8$.

tools.name: Arrangements with repeats
tools.why: Swapping identical cubes gives the same tower, so divide out those swaps.

tools.name: A bijection with a longer object
tools.why: Each $8$-tower plus its unique leftover cube on top gives a $9$-tower, and removing the top cube of a $9$-tower gives back the $8$-tower.

2019A17.approach: Casework on which colour is left out works, but there is a cleaner view: put the leftover cube on top. Every $8$-cube tower becomes exactly one $9$-cube tower using all cubes, and vice versa. So count arrangements of all $9$ cubes.

steps.title: See the correspondence
steps.explain: Given an $8$-tower, exactly one cube remains, and its colour is determined. Put it on top to make a $9$-tower. Conversely, removing the top cube of any $9$-tower gives a valid $8$-tower. This pairs the two kinds of towers one to one.

check.q: With $1$ red and $2$ blue cubes, how many $2$-cube towers are there?

steps.title: Count the $9$-towers
steps.explain: Arranging $2$ red, $3$ blue, $4$ green in a row: $\dfrac{9!}{2!\,3!\,4!}=\dfrac{362880}{2\cdot6\cdot24}=1260$.

steps.title: Check by casework
steps.explain: Leaving out red: $\tfrac{8!}{1!3!4!}=280$; blue: $\tfrac{8!}{2!2!4!}=420$; green: $\tfrac{8!}{2!3!3!}=560$. Total $1260$, as expected.

2019A17.bridge: Put the leftover cube on top and count arrangements of all nine cubes.
solution: Adding the unused cube on top turns each $8$-tower into a unique $9$-tower using all cubes, and removing the top cube reverses this.
So the count equals the number of arrangements of $2$ red, $3$ blue, $4$ green cubes.
2019A17.shortcut: Remember the trick: "use all but one" arrangements equal arrangements of all of them.
traps: Using $8!$ divided by the factorials of the original counts (not valid, since one cube is missing).
Forgetting that the colour left out can be any of the three.
2019A17.recognize: Arrangements that use all but one of a multiset: append the leftover item to make a full arrangement. Bijections often turn messy casework into one formula.

2019A18.goal: In base $k$, the repeating expansion $0.\overline{23}_k$ equals $\tfrac7{51}$. We convert the repeating base-$k$ number into a fraction in $k$ and solve.

tools.name: Repeating expansion as a fraction
tools.why: Multiply $x=0.\overline{ab}_k$ by $k^2$: $k^2x=ab.\overline{ab}_k$, subtract to get $(k^2-1)x=ak+b$.

tools.name: Factoring the quadratic
tools.why: Cross-multiplying gives a quadratic with an integer root.

2019A18.approach: Turn the repeating number into a fraction exactly as in base ten: shifting by two places multiplies by $k^2$. Set it equal to $\tfrac7{51}$ and solve the quadratic, keeping the positive integer root (and $k>3$ since digit $3$ appears).

steps.title: Convert the repeating number
steps.explain: Let $x=0.\overline{23}_k$. Then $k^2x=23.\overline{23}_k$, so $k^2x-x=2k+3$ and $x=\dfrac{2k+3}{k^2-1}$.

steps.title: Solve
steps.explain: The discriminant is $102^2+4\cdot7\cdot160=10404+4480=14884=122^2$. So $k=\tfrac{102\pm122}{14}$, and the positive root is $\tfrac{224}{14}=16$. Check: $\tfrac{35}{255}=\tfrac7{51}$.

2019A18.bridge: Write $0.\overline{23}_k=\tfrac{2k+3}{k^2-1}$, set it equal to $\tfrac7{51}$, and solve.
2019A18.shortcut: Test the choices: $k^2-1$ must make $\tfrac{2k+3}{k^2-1}$ reduce to sevenths over $51=3\cdot17$; $k=16$ gives $\tfrac{35}{255}$ immediately.
traps: Dividing by $k^2$ instead of $k^2-1$.
Reading $23_k$ as twenty-three instead of $2k+3$.
2019A18.recognize: Repeating expansions in any base convert like repeating decimals: shift by the period length and subtract.

2019A19.goal: We minimise $(x+1)(x+2)(x+3)(x+4)+2019$ over real $x$. A degree-$4$ product looks hard, but pairing factors turns it into a quadratic in a new variable.

tools.name: Pair outer and inner factors
tools.why: Both pairs have the same $x^2+5x$ part, so a single substitution handles both.

tools.name: Difference of squares
tools.why: Centre the substitution between the two pairs.

tools.name: Minimum of a square
tools.why: Squares are never negative.

2019A19.approach: Do not expand the product. Notice that the factors are symmetric about $-2.5$, so pair the outer two and the inner two: both become $x^2+5x+\text{constant}$. Substitute $u=x^2+5x+5$ (the average of the two pairs) and the product becomes $u^2-1$.

check.q: What is $(x+1)(x+3)$ paired with $(x+2)^2$ in terms of $v=x^2+4x$?

steps.title: Minimise
steps.explain: $u^2-1\ge-1$, with equality when $u=0$. We need $x^2+5x+5=0$ to have real solutions: its discriminant is $25-20=5>0$, so yes.

steps.title: Add the constant
steps.explain: The least value of the expression is $-1+2019=2018$.

check.q: If the minimum of $f$ is $-1$, what is the minimum of $f+2019$?
check.why: Adding a constant shifts the minimum.

2019A19.bridge: Pair the factors into $(u-1)(u+1)$ and minimise $u^2-1$.
solution: $u=0$ is achievable since $x^2+5x+5=0$ has real roots.
2019A19.shortcut: For four equally spaced linear factors, pair the outer and inner ones and centre the substitution; the minimum of the product is always $-1\cdot(\text{spacing})^4$ here.
traps: Plugging in $x=-2.5$ (the centre): that gives $\tfrac{9}{16}$, not the minimum.
Expanding to a quartic and trying calculus.
2019A19.recognize: Products of evenly spaced factors: pair them symmetrically so a common quadratic appears, then substitute.

2019A20.goal: Placing $1$–$9$ in a $3\times3$ grid at random, we want the probability that every row sum and every column sum is odd. Only which cells hold odd numbers matters.

tools.name: Parity of a sum
tools.fact: \text{A sum is odd}\iff\text{it has an odd number of odd terms}
tools.why: Even terms do not change parity; each odd term flips it.

tools.name: Counting positions
tools.fact: \binom95=126\text{ equally likely sets of cells for the }5\text{ odd numbers}
tools.why: By symmetry each choice of $5$ cells for the odds is equally likely.

2019A20.approach: Forget the actual numbers: there are $5$ odd numbers ($1,3,5,7,9$) and $4$ even ones. A row sum is odd iff the row contains $1$ or $3$ odd numbers. Find all placements of the $5$ odds that make every row and column have an odd count, and divide by $\binom95$.

steps.title: Row counts
steps.explain: Each row has $1$ or $3$ odds, and the three rows total $5$. The only option is $3+1+1$ in some order. Same for columns.

check.q: Three odd numbers from $\{1,3\}$ add to $5$. Which multiset works?

steps.title: The pattern
steps.explain: One row is all odd and one column is all odd. That is already $3+3-1=5$ cells (they share one cell), using all five odds. The other cells are even, and each row and column then has $1$ or $3$ odds. So the odds form a "cross" of a full row and a full column: $3\cdot3=9$ patterns.

check.q: How many cells are in a full row together with a full column of a $3\times3$ grid?
check.why: $3+3-1$, since they overlap in one cell.

steps.title: Probability
steps.explain: $\dfrac{9}{\binom95}=\dfrac9{126}=\dfrac1{14}$.

2019A20.bridge: Reduce to placing $5$ odd numbers; find the cross patterns and divide by $\binom95$.
solution: Only parity matters; the $5$ odd numbers occupy a uniformly random set of $5$ cells.
Each row and column needs an odd number of odds, so the counts are $3,1,1$ for rows and for columns.
That forces one full row and one full column of odds: $3\cdot3=9$ patterns.
2019A20.shortcut: Probability problems about sums being odd or even: replace numbers by parities and count patterns.
traps: Counting arrangements of all $9!$ numbers without noticing the parities are what matter (fine, but much longer).
Missing that the full row and column overlap in one cell.
2019A20.recognize: Conditions on parity of row and column sums reduce to placing the odd entries; small grids then allow a direct pattern count.

2019A21.goal: A triangle with sides $15,15,24$ has all three sides tangent to a sphere of radius $6$. We want the distance from the sphere's centre to the triangle's plane.

tools.name: Plane section of a sphere
tools.fact: \text{A plane at distance }h\text{ from the centre cuts a circle of radius }\sqrt{R^2-h^2}
tools.why: Pythagoras on the radius to any point of the circle.

tools.name: The incircle
tools.fact: \text{The circle tangent to all three sides in the triangle's plane is the incircle.}
tools.why: The sphere touches each side at one point, and those points lie on the circle where the sphere meets the plane.

tools.name: Inradius
tools.why: Split the triangle into three triangles from the incentre, each with height $r$.

2019A21.approach: The sphere meets the triangle's plane in a circle, and that circle touches all three sides, so it is the incircle. Find the inradius from area and semiperimeter, then use Pythagoras with the sphere's radius.

steps.title: Area and semiperimeter
steps.explain: The isosceles triangle with base $24$ has height $\sqrt{15^2-12^2}=9$, so area $\tfrac12\cdot24\cdot9=108$. The semiperimeter is $\tfrac{15+15+24}2=27$.

check.q: What is the height to the base of a triangle with sides $10,10,12$?

steps.title: Inradius
steps.explain: $r=\tfrac{108}{27}=4$. This is the radius of the circle in which the sphere meets the plane.

check.q: A triangle has area $24$ and semiperimeter $12$. What is its inradius?

steps.title: Distance to the plane
steps.explain: By Pythagoras, $h=\sqrt{6^2-4^2}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt5$.

check.q: A sphere of radius $5$ meets a plane in a circle of radius $3$. How far is the plane from the centre?

2019A21.bridge: The sphere cuts the plane in the incircle; find its radius and use Pythagoras.
solution: The triangle has height $9$ on base $24$: area $108$, semiperimeter $27$.
The sphere meets the plane in a circle tangent to all three sides, which is the incircle, radius $4$.
2019A21.shortcut: $15$-$15$-$24$ is two $9$-$12$-$15$ right triangles glued together, so the area is immediate.
traps: Using the circumradius instead of the inradius.
Answering $4$ (the inradius) instead of the distance.
2019A21.recognize: A sphere tangent to a polygon's sides: its intersection with the plane is the polygon's incircle. Then sphere radius, circle radius and distance form a right triangle.

2019A22.goal: Each of $x,y$ is $0$ with probability $\tfrac14$, $1$ with probability $\tfrac14$, or uniform on $[0,1]$ with probability $\tfrac12$. We want $P(|x-y|>\tfrac12)$. Split by what kind each number is.

tools.name: Law of total probability
tools.why: The cases (endpoint/endpoint, endpoint/uniform, uniform/uniform) cover everything without overlap.

tools.name: Probability as area
tools.why: In the unit square the region is two corner triangles with legs $\tfrac12$, total area $2\cdot\tfrac18$.

2019A22.approach: Each number is "$0$", "$1$" or "uniform". List the type combinations with their probabilities, find the conditional probability of $|x-y|>\tfrac12$ for each, and add.

steps.title: Both endpoints
steps.explain: $|x-y|>\tfrac12$ only if one is $0$ and the other is $1$: probability $2\cdot\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac18$. (Both $0$ or both $1$ gives difference $0$.)

steps.title: One endpoint, one uniform
steps.explain: This happens with probability $2\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac12$. If the endpoint is $0$, we need the uniform number $>\tfrac12$: probability $\tfrac12$; similarly for $1$. Contribution $\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac14$.

check.q: If $x=0$ and $y$ is uniform on $[0,1]$, what is $P(|x-y|>\tfrac12)$?

steps.title: Both uniform
steps.explain: Probability $\tfrac14$ that both are uniform; then $P(|x-y|>\tfrac12)=\tfrac14$ (two corner triangles of the unit square). Contribution $\tfrac1{16}$. Total $\tfrac18+\tfrac14+\tfrac1{16}=\tfrac{7}{16}$.

2019A22.bridge: Split by the type of each number, find each conditional probability, and add.
solution: One $0$ and one $1$: probability $\tfrac18$, always works.
One endpoint and one uniform: probability $\tfrac12$, works half the time: $\tfrac14$.
Both uniform: probability $\tfrac14$, works $\tfrac14$ of the time: $\tfrac1{16}$.
2019A22.shortcut: Draw the unit square once for the uniform–uniform case: the region $|x-y|>\tfrac12$ is two triangles of area $\tfrac18$.
traps: Treating the endpoint cases as continuous (they have positive probability).
Forgetting the factor $2$ for which of $x,y$ is the endpoint.
2019A22.recognize: Mixed discrete/continuous random variables: condition on the type, use counting for the discrete parts and area for the continuous parts.

2019A23.goal: The children say $1,2,3,\ldots$ in turns of lengths $1,2,3,\ldots$, rotating Tadd, Todd, Tucker. We want the $2019$th number Tadd says. Tadd speaks on turns $1,4,7,\ldots$, saying $1,4,7,\ldots$ numbers.

tools.name: Arithmetic series
tools.why: Average of first and last term times the number of terms.

tools.name: Triangular numbers
tools.why: After $t$ turns in total, the last number said is $\tfrac{t(t+1)}2$.

2019A23.approach: Count how many numbers Tadd has said after his $m$th turn. Find which of Tadd's turns contains his $2019$th number. Then find where that turn ends overall and count back.

steps.title: Tadd's running total
steps.explain: Tadd's $m$th turn is overall turn $3m-2$, of length $3m-2$. After $m$ turns he has said $\tfrac{m(3m-1)}2$ numbers. For $m=36$: $\tfrac{36\cdot107}{2}=1926$; for $m=37$: $\tfrac{37\cdot110}2=2035$. So the $2019$th is in his $37$th turn.

steps.title: Where that turn ends
steps.explain: Tadd's $37$th turn is overall turn $3\cdot37-2=109$. After $109$ turns the last number said is $\tfrac{109\cdot110}2=5995$. So Tadd's $2035$th number is $5995$.

check.q: After $10$ turns in total, what is the last number said?

steps.title: Count back
steps.explain: The $2019$th is $2035-2019=16$ numbers earlier within the same turn: $5995-16=5979$.

check.q: If the $50$th item is $300$ and items are consecutive, what is the $45$th?

2019A23.bridge: Find which of Tadd's turns contains his $2019$th number, where that turn ends, and count back.
solution: After $m$ turns Tadd has said $\tfrac{m(3m-1)}2$ numbers; $m=37$ gives $2035\ge2019>1926$.
His $37$th turn is turn $109$ overall, ending at $\tfrac{109\cdot110}2=5995$.
traps: Off-by-one when counting back within the turn.
Using Tadd's turn number $37$ instead of the overall turn $109$ for the triangular number.
2019A23.recognize: "The $N$th item said by a player" in a growing-turn game: sum the player's turn lengths to locate the turn, then use the global count to find the value.

2019A24.goal: $\tfrac1{f(s)}$ for the cubic $f$ with roots $p,q,r$ is split into partial fractions $\tfrac{A}{s-p}+\cdots$. We need $\tfrac1A+\tfrac1B+\tfrac1C$. Find each coefficient in terms of the roots, then use Vieta.

tools.name: Cover-up rule for partial fractions
tools.why: Multiply by $s-p$ and let $s\to p$: the other terms vanish and $\tfrac{s-p}{f(s)}\to\tfrac1{(p-q)(p-r)}$.

tools.name: Vieta for a cubic
tools.why: For $x^3-ax^2+bx-c$ the roots satisfy $\sum p=a$, $\sum pq=b$.

tools.name: Symmetric expression
tools.why: Expand $(p+q+r)^2=\sum p^2+2\sum pq$.

2019A24.approach: You never need the actual roots. Use the cover-up rule to write $\tfrac1A=(p-q)(p-r)$ and similarly for $B$ and $C$. Add the three, simplify into a symmetric expression, and evaluate with Vieta.

steps.title: Find $	frac1A$
steps.explain: $f(s)=(s-p)(s-q)(s-r)$. Multiply the identity by $s-p$ and set $s=p$: $A=\tfrac1{(p-q)(p-r)}$, so $\tfrac1A=(p-q)(p-r)$. Similarly $\tfrac1B=(q-p)(q-r)$ and $\tfrac1C=(r-p)(r-q)$.

steps.title: Add and simplify
steps.explain: Expanding, $(p-q)(p-r)+(q-p)(q-r)+(r-p)(r-q)=p^2+q^2+r^2-pq-qr-rp$.

2019A24.bridge: Use the cover-up rule for each coefficient, add the reciprocals, and evaluate with Vieta.
2019A24.shortcut: $\tfrac1A=f'(p)$ (derivative of the cubic at the root), so the sum is $\sum f'(p)=3\sum p^2-44\sum p+240$, which also gives $244$.
traps: Trying to find the roots numerically.
Sign errors in $(q-p)(q-r)$.
2019A24.recognize: Expressions in roots you cannot find: rewrite them as symmetric polynomials and use Vieta.

2019A25.goal: For $1\le n\le50$, when is $\dfrac{(n^2-1)!}{(n!)^n}$ an integer? Relate it to a quantity that is known to be an integer, and find exactly when the leftover factor causes trouble.

tools.name: Splitting objects into groups
tools.why: It counts the ways to split $n^2$ objects into $n$ unlabelled groups of $n$.

tools.name: Rewriting the expression
tools.why: Multiply and divide by $n^2$ and by $n!$.

tools.name: Powers of a prime in a factorial (Legendre)
tools.why: Count multiples of $p$, of $p^2$, and so on.

2019A25.approach: The given fraction is an integer times $\tfrac{n!}{n^2}$. When $n^2\mid n!$, it is certainly an integer. For the remaining $n$ (primes and $n=4$), check directly with prime powers that it fails.

steps.title: When is $n^2mid n!$?
steps.explain: For composite $n=ab$ with $1<a<b<n$, both $a,b$ and $n$ itself appear in $n!$, giving $n^2\mid n!$. For $n=p^2$ with $p>2$, $p$ and $2p$ both appear, so $p^4\mid n!$ too. It fails for $n$ prime ($n!$ has only one factor $n$) and for $n=4$ ($4!=24$). It holds for $n=1$.

steps.title: Primes fail
steps.explain: For $n=p$ prime, $(p^2-1)!$ contains the multiples $p,2p,\ldots,(p-1)p$: exactly $p-1$ factors of $p$. The denominator $(p!)^p$ has $p$ factors of $p$. So it is not an integer.

check.q: How many factors of $5$ are in $24!$?

steps.title: $n=4$ fails; count
steps.explain: $\tfrac{15!}{(4!)^4}$: $15!$ has $7+3+1=11$ factors of $2$, while $24^4$ has $12$. Not an integer. So the failures are the $15$ primes up to $50$ and $n=4$: $16$ values, leaving $50-16=34$.

check.q: How many primes are at most $50$?

2019A25.bridge: Write the fraction as an integer times $\tfrac{n!}{n^2}$, then check the exceptions $n$ prime and $n=4$.
solution: $\tfrac{(n^2-1)!}{(n!)^n}=\tfrac{(n^2)!}{(n!)^{n+1}}\cdot\tfrac{n!}{n^2}$, and the first factor is an integer (group-splitting count).
So it is an integer whenever $n^2\mid n!$, which holds for $n=1$ and every composite $n\ne4$.
For prime $p$, the numerator has $p-1$ factors of $p$ but the denominator has $p$: not an integer.
For $n=4$: $11$ factors of $2$ versus $12$: not an integer.
2019A25.shortcut: Guess "fails exactly for primes and $4$" from small cases, then subtract: $50-16=34$.
traps: Forgetting $n=4$, the one composite with $n^2\nmid n!$.
Counting $1$ as prime.
2019A25.recognize: Integrality of factorial ratios: compare with a known combinatorial count, then handle leftover factors with prime-power counting.
